newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran aims to lift petrochemical output, exports.
newsitem.headline: Iran aims to lift petrochemical output, exports.

text.p: Iran's petrochemical output will rise to 11.5 million tonnes in the next Iranian year from a projected 10.5 million tonnes in the current year, Iranian Deputy Oil Minister Ahmad Rahgozar said on Tuesday.

Petrochemical export revenue -- mainly in sales to Central Asia and China -- would rise to $650 million in the year which starts on March 21, from a forecast $500 million in the current year, said Rahgozar who is also president of the National Petrochemical Company (NPC).
"This is thanks to the implementation of 10 major expansion and development contracts in the first five-year plan (1989-1994)," Rahgozar told Reuters.
NPC planned six major projects in the current second five-year plan (1995-2000) which would boost annual petrochemical exports earnings to $2 billion, he said.
Five of these projects include expanding plastics and MTBE gasoline oxygenate capacity at the 3.85 million tonnes a year Bandar Khomeini plant, Iran's largest petrochemicals facility.
The sixth is expanding acetic acid and methanol capacity at the 430,000 tonne Kharg Island plant.
The first units to come on stream within the next two years would be a 633,000 tonne capacity methanol plant at Kharg Island and a 150,000 tonne polyxylene facility at Bandar Khomeini, Rahgozar said.
Commissioning of the 500,000 tonnes Tabriz plant is expected to begin in March, two years behind schedule.
NPC was also in talks with companies from France, the Netherlands and Austria on setting up joint ventures in a fertiliser and plastics plant in Iran.
Iran previously had foreign joint venture partners in its petrochemical sector but these companies left after the 1979 Islamic revolution and its 1980-1988 war with Iraq.
"We are prepared to form joint ventures with foreign investors...we hope to reach an agreement in six months," Rahgozar said, adding that the Iranian side would hold 51 percent.
NPC's 25-year strategic plan calls for the construction of 30 complexes at a cost of $12 billion to boost capacity to 30 million tonnes a year.
Iran currently imports $200 million worth of petrochemicals, mainly in the form of polypropylene, natural rubber and chemicals for industry, he said.
The state petrochemical company has $800 million of debt to pay off in the next two years.
Iran's 11 petrochemical production complexes make the country the second largest petrochemical producer in the Middle East behind Saudi Arabia.
